extracted.intended_audience: artisans and natural philosophers (surveyors, potters, miners, metallurgists) in a pre-modern technical context
extracted.subtask_short: surveying and material selection for artisans
extracted.subtask_description: Practical instructions and evaluative criteria for measuring celestial altitudes and shadows, setting up instruments, selecting and assessing clays/ceramics, locating metal deposits, and methods for producing fresh water — aimed at craftspeople and natural philosophers who must apply measurements and choose materials. Contains geometric procedures, instrument-setup rules, material classifications, and environmental criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use solar-shadow geometry for building orientation and seasonal insolation
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure the paths/arcs of the Sun and the perpendicularity of its rays to determine where and when walls/roofs will receive or lack heat (e.g. to ensure winter heating of houses).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct two concentric circles (one smaller, one larger) and compare arcs; identify the quarter/arc portions that correspond to the winter position of the Sun (hyemalis). Use these arcs to ensure that at mid-day in winter rays perpendicular to surfaces will be received so that buildings gain heat and sustain crops/comfort. The text gives explicit construction of arcs and selecting the arc whose perpetual annual perpendicular incidence will allow winter vegetables and fruits to be preserved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Orient plane mirrors (planispecula) so reflection is perpendicular
rubrics_metrics.description: To make a plane mirror reflect Sun-rays perpendicularly, orient the mirror so the perpendicular from the Sun's centre to the mirror coincides with the perpendicular that passes from the Earth's centre to the mirror's plane.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the Sun is placed so that a perpendicular from its center to an extended surface meets the plane of the mirror as a right line, then rays from the Sun will strike and be reflected perpendicularly as intended. The page explains thinking in terms of 'center of Sun' and 'center of Earth' and the necessary orthogonality; practical instruction: imagine/protract the solid angle and align the mirror's plane accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for Earth's curvature and Sun's finite size when interpreting shadows
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not assume rays are strictly perpendicular or parallel across extended planes because Earth's curvature and the Sun's finite diameter alter ray directions and shadow shapes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text warns that because the Earth is round (not planar) and because rays do not all tend to the Earth's centre in the same way, shadows and reflections deviate from simple planar expectations. Corrections must be applied when interpreting shadow lengths and directions: only near the observer can some simplifications be assumed; for larger distances the curvature and non-parallelism of rays matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure heights/altitudes using a rod (virga) and circle with chord/arcuate tables
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine the altitude (of the Sun or a star) and hence heights/distances by placing a vertical rod, measuring its shadow (umbra), and using chord-and-arc (trigonometric) tables to obtain the angle and related proportions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fix a rod perpendicular to a prepared plane; measure the length of its shadow off the plane. Use the proportion of the rod to the shadow (AF to AD) and a table of chord and arc to find the corresponding angle in the triangle (angle of altitude). From this angle and known proportions one computes distances in passuum (paces). The treatise gives stepwise arithmetic recipes (for example, methods to convert minute-angles into proportional heights) and warns about errors if the rod or plane are not truly perpendicular.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure instrument setup is truly perpendicular using iron ring and plumbs
rubrics_metrics.description: When establishing the measuring plane and the vertical rod, use mechanical means to guarantee true perpendicularity so geometric measurements are valid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mount a rod into a circular iron ring and fasten plumb-bobs or perpendicular weights at four sides beneath the plane so that the plane is truly flat and the rod truly orthogonal to it. If the ring, plumb lines and supporting board are set so that the perpendicular rod touches the plane equally from all sides, then the plane is suitable for accurate altitude/umbra measurement. If the circle does not bear perpendiculars at every point the plane is not suitable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arithmetic procedure for converting measured minute-angles to altitude proportions
rubrics_metrics.description: When the measured angular minutes (of a star's apparent diameter or an angle) are small, apply a specific proportional arithmetic correction before using tables to find altitude/diameter proportions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text prescribes a recipe: duplicate the measured minutes, add a nineteenth part, then repeatedly divide by specified large constants (the text gives an algorithm involving dividing by 7200 and then using tabular proportions) to convert minute-measurements into proportion of altitude to diameter. This is presented as a laborious but reliable arithmetical method for deducing altitudes from small measured angles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify materials by behaviour under heat (succus, lapis, metallum, terra)
rubrics_metrics.description: Categorize earths and materials into four genera based on whether they liquefy, return to original form, can be drawn or bent (ductility), or are permanently solid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a material liquefies and returns to its form, it is termed a 'soccus' (sucus). If it does not liquefy and is very hard (not ductile, easily fractured), it is a 'lapis' (stone). If it can be drawn/ductile (e.g., bitumen can be drawn), it is a 'metallum'. If it does not liquefy but is softer and passes into minute parts, it is 'terra' (earth). From these four, many composite genera (mixtures of these) are derived; examples are given (sucus = sulphur; lapis = crystal; terra = Lemnian earth; metallum = silver).

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria to recognize and select pottery clay (qualities of good vases)
rubrics_metrics.description: Good clay for vases should be very light and fine, not exuding liquids, resistant to firing, not easily broken, and capable of producing a glossy, attractive finish with suitable colors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The treatise lists five virtues for clay: be the lightest (tenuissima), not exude (non forbeant/exudet), not easily fractured (non facile frangantur), withstand fire (ignibus refillant/resist), and not exude liquids. Additional practical notes: avoid too translucent or pale ware (pallere is a defect); avoid warty protuberances; prefer smooth, fat (pingue) clays that yield shine (nitor) and desired colors (purpurea, candidus); provenance and preparation (beating, mixing with herbs, repeated pounding and drying) affect final quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for high-quality myrrhina/procellana (porcelain)
rubrics_metrics.description: Valuable myrrhina/procellana should be thin, fine, sometimes translucent, with a pleasing color (from purple to white variants), a fine surface gloss, and stability (not easily exuding or breaking); provenance and preparation affect value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Myrrhina (what later would be called porcelain) is praised when very thin and of fine density, sometimes translucent, and when it acquires varied colors under firing (purpureous red, white, etc.). Odour and local provenance (e.g., India, Carmania, Lemnos) are noted historically; the text also explains how overuse and cheap imitation degrade the quality and price. Practical preparation includes selecting suitable clay, repeated pounding, mixing with organic liquids, and careful firing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Locate metal deposits preferentially in mountains and exposed ground
rubrics_metrics.description: Metals and gem generation are more likely in mountainous regions where substrata are solid, deeper, less exhausted by cultivation, and subject to favourable heat and drainage conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author argues mountains are better for discovering metallic veins because: (1) their depth and solidity preserve generating forces; (2) they are not exhausted by ploughing and human industry; (3) they store and concentrate heat and appropriate humours; (4) their slopes and exposures allow easier discovery of veins and derivation of water and earth already loosened. By contrast, in plains metals may be present but concealed and harder to locate, and searching is more laborious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Environmental conditions favourable to metallic generation
rubrics_metrics.description: Metal generation (formation) requires a particular balance of humidity and heat: warm and suitably humid (but not excessively aqueous) localities favour metallic production; cold/wet regions hinder it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text states that metallic generation needs moist (aqueous) yet warm conditions so that the humid matter becomes 'fat' and is transformed by heat; excessive water impedes generation. Thus warm regions and mountain slopes with flowing waters that are not stagnant are most productive. The fertility of soil and presence of certain waters influence metallic abundance and the quality of gems formed (drier, warmer places produce better gems).

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods to derive fresh water from the sea
rubrics_metrics.description: Three principal methods are described to obtain fresh water from seawater: allow it to settle (descend), coagulate/force (typically by heating or inducing coagulation), and percolate it through materials; a fourth speculative method is to blunt the sharpness of salt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The treatise lists: (1) let the brine descend/settle so heavier saline parts sink and clearer water remain; (2) coagulate by heating (cogatur) causing separation; (3) percolate through filtering media (percoletur); and (4) possibly use agents to blunt the saltiness. It also mentions practical experiments: using vessels to entrap the fresh layer, distillation by heating (evaporation and condensation), and the attraction of oils or fats in certain setups—practical recipes and cautions follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish types of mixture (mistio) and tests for perfect mixture
rubrics_metrics.description: Different modes of mixing are named and distinguished (generation, crafis, mixture, fermentation, heap); not all indicate true incorporation of forms, and empirical tests show imperfect mixing of liquids like wine and water.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text defines: generation (mutant forms into new forms), crafis (where forms remain), mixture (e.g., wine with water where wine's form persists), fermentation, and heaps (accumulation). It gives an empirical test: when a linen cloth is dipped into wine-and-water, wine reappears on the cloth showing that true homogeneous mixing did not occur. Thus one must not assume simple blending produces single substance; forms often persist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical rules for mixing oil, wine, and water and expectations about layering
rubrics_metrics.description: When combining liquids such as oil, wine, and water, layering and perceived mixture depend on relative lightness, temperature, and sequence of addition; heating and evaporation alter outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observations: oil tends to float over wine; wine floats over water according to relative lightness and specific gravities. To combine oil and water for disappearance of water one may heat to evaporate water before adding oil; when mixing oil and wine in a vessel, one should allow the water to be expelled by heat so oil can be integrated. The text explains why an oil layer may burn or disperse and why clarity and transparency relate to fatness and fineness. Practical steps: warm the vessel, remove water by heating, then add oil; or expect layering where lighter liquids will remain atop heavier ones.
